questions.q: Which statement best characterizes peripheral arterial disease (PAD)?
ch: Lymphatic obstruction producing non-pitting limb swelling with thickened overlying skin
Atherosclerotic narrowing of the limb arteries causing exertional claudication and marking systemic cardiovascular risk
Venous valve incompetence producing dependent edema and stasis pigmentation of the calf
Inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis confined to the digital arteries of the hands
Acute thrombosis of the deep calf veins presenting with unilateral swelling and tenderness
questions.exp: PAD is atherosclerosis of the limb arteries — the same plaque as coronary disease — producing a supply-demand mismatch: flow is adequate at rest but insufficient during exertion, which is intermittent claudication. It is a coronary heart disease risk equivalent.
why: Non-pitting swelling with thickened skin is lymphedema, which does not produce claudication or absent pulses.
Dependent edema with stasis pigmentation describes chronic venous insufficiency, not arterial occlusive disease.
PAD is atherosclerotic plaque in the large and medium limb arteries, not a small-vessel vasculitis of the hands.
Acute unilateral calf swelling and tenderness is deep vein thrombosis; PAD causes exertional pain with diminished pulses.

questions.q: Which resting ankle-brachial index (ABI) value is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease?
questions.exp: A resting ankle-brachial index of 0.90 or less is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease; the index is the ratio of ankle systolic to the higher brachial systolic pressure.
why: This is the borderline range, not the diagnostic cutoff for peripheral arterial disease.
This is a normal resting ankle-brachial index.
This is a normal resting ankle-brachial index and does not establish the diagnosis.
A value above 1.40 suggests non-compressible, calcified vessels rather than health, and is not the diagnostic cutoff.

questions.q: Which set of findings makes up the '6 Ps' of acute limb ischemia?
ch: Pain, pruritus, purpura, pallor, pitting edema, pulsatility
Pallor, palpitations, pyrexia, paralysis, petechiae, pain
Paresthesia, pyuria, pallor, pain, photophobia, pulselessness
Pain, pallor, polyuria, pulselessness, pruritus, paresis
Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia
questions.exp: The 6 Ps of acute limb ischemia are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia (cold) — a surgical emergency requiring urgent anticoagulation and revascularization.
why: Pruritus, purpura, and pitting edema are not features of acute arterial occlusion.
Palpitations, pyrexia, and petechiae are not part of the acute limb ischemia mnemonic.
Pyuria and photophobia have nothing to do with limb perfusion.
Polyuria and pruritus are not among the six; paresthesia and poikilothermia are.

questions.q: A man with long-standing diabetes and chronic kidney disease has classic calf claudication, but his resting ABI is 1.48. What is the best next step?
ch: Proceed directly to surgical bypass of the femoropopliteal segment
Obtain CT angiography of the lower extremities as a screening test
Toe-brachial index, because medial calcification makes the ankle vessels non-compressible
Repeat the resting ABI in one week and accept the result if it is unchanged
Reassure him that an ABI above 1.40 excludes peripheral arterial disease
questions.exp: An ABI above 1.40 means non-compressible, medially calcified vessels — common in diabetes and chronic kidney disease — not healthy arteries. The toe-brachial index (TBI ≤0.70) is used when the ABI is falsely elevated by medial calcification.
why: Revascularization is not undertaken before the diagnosis is confirmed and medical therapy tried.
Anatomic imaging is reserved for planning revascularization, not for screening or diagnosis.
Repeating the same falsely elevated measurement does not overcome medial calcification.
An ABI above 1.40 indicates non-compressible calcified vessels, not the absence of disease.

questions.q: Which agent is the first-line symptomatic drug to increase pain-free walking distance in claudication, yet is contraindicated in heart failure?
ch: Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist
Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor
Cilostazol, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor
Low-dose aspirin, an antiplatelet agent
Atorvastatin, a high-intensity statin
questions.exp: Cilostazol is the first-line symptomatic drug for claudication, increasing pain-free walking distance, but as a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor it is contraindicated in heart failure — a favorite exam trap.
why: Warfarin has no role in stable claudication and is not a symptomatic agent.
An ACE inhibitor is used for blood pressure and cardiovascular risk reduction, not for walking distance.
Aspirin reduces MI, stroke, and cardiovascular death in symptomatic PAD but does not improve walking distance.
A statin stabilizes plaque and lowers LDL; it is not a symptomatic claudication drug.

questions.q: A 64-year-old smoker reports cramping buttock and hip pain with walking, erectile dysfunction, and absent femoral pulses. Where is the lesion?
ch: Infrapopliteal tibial disease
Isolated dorsalis pedis occlusion
Subclavian artery stenosis
Aortoiliac disease — Leriche syndrome
Femoropopliteal disease
questions.exp: Buttock and hip claudication with impotence and absent femoral pulses localizes the lesion to the aortoiliac segment — Leriche syndrome.
why: Distal tibial disease produces foot and calf symptoms, and the femoral pulses remain palpable.
An isolated pedal occlusion cannot explain buttock claudication or loss of the femoral pulse.
Subclavian disease affects the arm, not the buttock, hip, or erectile function.
Femoropopliteal disease causes calf claudication, not buttock pain with absent femoral pulses.

questions.q: Which treatment for intermittent claudication is a Class I, guideline first-line recommendation that improves walking distance as much as many drugs?
ch: Chronic warfarin anticoagulation targeting an INR of 2 to 3
Graduated compression stockings worn during all waking hours
Elevating both legs above heart level for an hour each day
Supervised exercise therapy — a structured walking program
Strict bed rest until the leg pain resolves completely
questions.exp: Supervised exercise therapy is a Class I, first-line recommendation: the patient walks to near-maximal claudication pain, rests, and repeats. It improves walking distance as much as many drugs.
why: Anticoagulation is not the treatment for stable claudication and adds bleeding risk.
Compression stockings treat venous disease and can worsen arterial perfusion.
Elevating an ischemic leg reduces perfusion — ischemic legs are kept dependent, below the heart.
Bed rest deconditions the patient; exertional claudication pain is expected and therapeutic, not harmful.

questions.q: A patient with known PAD now wakes at night with foot pain that improves when he hangs the foot off the side of the bed. What does this indicate?
ch: Critical limb-threatening ischemia with rest pain, needing urgent vascular referral
Simple nocturnal leg cramps requiring only stretching and better hydration
Improving collateral circulation and a favorable response to a walking program
Deep vein thrombosis of the calf, best confirmed with duplex ultrasound
Neurogenic pseudoclaudication arising from lumbar spinal stenosis
questions.exp: Rest pain that is worse lying flat and relieved by dangling the foot off the bed for gravity flow is advanced, critical limb-threatening ischemia, and it needs urgent vascular referral to save the limb.
why: Benign cramps are not relieved by gravity and do not occur in this pattern in a patient with known PAD.
Gravity-dependent relief signals inadequate resting perfusion, not improving collaterals.
Deep vein thrombosis causes swelling and tenderness, not pain relieved by dangling the foot.
Pseudoclaudication is exertional and relieved by flexion or sitting, not by dangling the foot at night.

questions.q: A 70-year-old has leg pain with walking that is relieved only by sitting or bending forward; his pedal pulses and ABI are normal. What is the most likely explanation?
ch: Atheroembolism causing blue toe syndrome, with mottled toes and intact proximal pulses
Neurogenic pseudoclaudication from spinal stenosis, relieved by flexion rather than by rest alone
Aortoiliac Leriche disease, which typically abolishes the femoral pulses and lowers the ABI
Critical limb-threatening ischemia, which causes rest pain and ulceration rather than exertional pain
Acute limb ischemia, which presents abruptly with the 6 Ps including pulselessness and pallor
questions.exp: Neurogenic pseudoclaudication from spinal stenosis is relieved by flexion or sitting rather than by standing rest alone, and the pulses and ABI are normal — the key mimic to distinguish from true claudication.
why: Blue toe syndrome presents with mottled discolored toes, which this patient does not have.
Leriche disease gives absent femoral pulses and an abnormal ABI; both are normal in this patient.
Critical ischemia causes rest pain and tissue loss with a very low ABI, not normal pulses.
Acute limb ischemia is sudden and dramatic, not a chronic reproducible walking complaint.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the prognosis of symptomatic PAD and the lipid goal that follows from it?
ch: PAD risk is confined to the limb, so the lipid target is the same as for the general population
Amputation is the leading cause of death in PAD, so a statin adds little beyond exercise therapy
Statins should be avoided in PAD because myalgias limit walking distance in claudication
Lipid lowering is indicated only after revascularization has failed to relieve the symptoms
PAD is a coronary heart disease risk equivalent — most patients die of MI or stroke — so a high-intensity statin targeting LDL below 70 mg/dL is recommended
questions.exp: PAD is a coronary heart disease risk equivalent: most patients die of MI or stroke, not limb loss. A high-intensity statin is recommended for essentially all PAD patients, targeting LDL below 70 mg/dL and by many accounts below 55.
why: PAD risk is systemic — the leg is the messenger, and the ABI speaks to the coronaries and carotids too.
Most PAD patients die of MI or stroke rather than limb loss, and statin therapy is central, not marginal.
A statin is recommended for essentially all PAD patients; myalgias are monitored, not a reason to withhold it.
Lipid lowering is core secondary prevention from the moment of diagnosis, independent of revascularization.

questions.q: Which mechanism best explains how elevated LDL-C causes atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease?
ch: Retained ApoB-containing particles enter the arterial intima, oxidize, and trigger foam-cell and plaque formation
Cholesterol crystals precipitate directly within the cardiac valves and produce stenosis
Excess circulating lipid raises blood viscosity enough to mechanically obstruct the arteries
Triglycerides are deposited within the myocardium and progressively impair contractile function
HDL particles carry cholesterol into the vessel wall, where it accumulates as fatty streaks
questions.exp: Retained ApoB-containing lipoprotein particles enter the arterial intima, oxidize, and trigger foam-cell and plaque formation — the basis of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
why: Valvular cholesterol crystal deposition is not the mechanism of atherosclerosis described here.
Viscosity does not mechanically obstruct arteries; retained ApoB particles in the intima drive plaque.
Myocardial triglyceride deposition is not the mechanism; very high triglycerides instead threaten pancreatitis.
HDL does not deposit cholesterol in the wall — the retained ApoB-containing particles do.

questions.q: A 32-year-old with an untreated LDL-C of 245 mg/dL has thickened Achilles tendons and firm nodules over the knuckles. What do these findings indicate?
ch: Corneal arcus, an entirely expected age-related change
Gouty tophi, reflecting chronically elevated serum uric acid
Tendon xanthomas, the classic sign of familial hypercholesterolemia
Eruptive xanthomas, which accompany severe hypertriglyceridemia
Xanthelasma, a periorbital deposit without lipid significance
questions.exp: Tendon xanthomas of the Achilles and knuckles are the classic sign of familial hypercholesterolemia; suspect it when untreated LDL-C is 190 mg/dL or higher, or with a strong premature-CAD family history.
why: Corneal arcus is a corneal ring, and in a young patient it is itself abnormal — it is not what is described.
Tophi are urate deposits of gout and are unrelated to an untreated LDL-C of 245 mg/dL.
Eruptive xanthomas go with very high triglycerides, not an isolated LDL-C elevation.
Xanthelasma is a periorbital lipid deposit and is a genuine clue to dyslipidemia, but it is not a tendon finding.

questions.q: By what mechanism do statins lower LDL-C?
ch: They activate PPAR-alpha and thereby accelerate triglyceride clearance
They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors
They block intestinal cholesterol absorption at the brush border
They inhibit ATP-citrate lyase upstream of hepatic cholesterol synthesis
They are monoclonal antibodies that neutralize circulating PCSK9
questions.exp: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors — which is also why PCSK9, the protein that degrades those receptors, matters so much.
why: Accelerating triglyceride clearance describes the fibrates, such as fenofibrate.
Blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption is the mechanism of ezetimibe.
ATP-citrate lyase inhibition is the mechanism of bempedoic acid.
Monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9 are evolocumab and alirocumab, not statins.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four AHA/ACC statin benefit groups?
ch: Isolated triglycerides of 200 mg/dL on a fasting panel
Any adult over the age of 40 regardless of risk factors
A total cholesterol above 180 mg/dL in a nonsmoking adult
Untreated LDL-C of 190 mg/dL or higher at any age
An HDL-C below 40 mg/dL in an otherwise healthy adult
questions.exp: The four statin benefit groups are clinical ASCVD, LDL-C of 190 mg/dL or higher, diabetes at age 40 to 75, and an elevated 10-year risk by the pooled cohort estimator.
why: Moderately elevated triglycerides alone are not a statin benefit group; they are a separate problem.
Age over 40 alone is not a benefit group — diabetes at age 40 to 75 is.
A total cholesterol threshold is not how the benefit groups are defined.
A low HDL-C by itself is not one of the four statin benefit groups.

questions.q: A patient's triglycerides return at 1,200 mg/dL and he has epigastric pain. Which risk does this represent, and which drug class targets it?
ch: Cholestatic liver injury — treated with observation and imaging
Acute pancreatitis — treated with a fibrate such as fenofibrate
Accelerated atherosclerosis — treated with a PCSK9 inhibitor
Rhabdomyolysis — treated by stopping all lipid-lowering therapy
Hypothyroid myopathy — treated with levothyroxine replacement
questions.exp: Severe hypertriglyceridemia above 500 mg/dL shifts the risk from atherosclerosis toward acute pancreatitis, and the primary target of a fibrate such as fenofibrate is very high triglycerides to prevent pancreatitis.
why: Cholestasis can raise lipids as a secondary cause, but it is not the risk this triglyceride level creates.
A PCSK9 inhibitor targets LDL-C; the immediate threat at this triglyceride level is pancreatitis.
Rhabdomyolysis is a rare statin adverse effect, not a consequence of very high triglycerides.
Hypothyroidism is a secondary cause of dyslipidemia but is not the acute risk in this presentation.

questions.q: Which drug combination carries the greatest risk of dangerous myopathy in a patient who needs both LDL and triglyceride lowering?
ch: Fenofibrate plus a statin
Ezetimibe plus a statin
Icosapent ethyl plus a statin
Bempedoic acid plus ezetimibe
Gemfibrozil plus a statin
questions.exp: Gemfibrozil combined with a statin is the dangerous myopathy combination; when a fibrate is needed with a statin, fenofibrate is used instead.
why: Fenofibrate is the fibrate chosen when one must be used with a statin, precisely because it is safer.
Ezetimibe with a statin is well tolerated and is the standard first add-on for additional LDL lowering.
Icosapent ethyl is added for residual risk with triglycerides of 150 to 499; its concerns are atrial fibrillation and bleeding.
Bempedoic acid is used in statin intolerance; its distinctive risks are raised uric acid and tendon rupture.

questions.q: A very high-risk ASCVD patient is not at LDL goal on a maximally tolerated high-intensity statin. What is the next step in the titration sequence?
ch: Stop the statin and start a fibrate as monotherapy instead
Add niacin and recheck the lipid panel in one year's time
Escalate the statin beyond the maximally tolerated dose
Defer any further therapy until a repeat CAC score is obtained
Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid if still not at goal
questions.exp: If the LDL goal is not met on a maximally tolerated statin, add ezetimibe — which blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption for a modest additional 15 to 20% reduction — then a PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid for very high-risk patients.
why: Stopping the statin sacrifices the largest source of LDL lowering and worsens ASCVD risk.
Niacin is not part of this titration sequence, and a one-year recheck is far too long an interval.
Exceeding the maximally tolerated dose is not the recommended move; add a nonstatin agent instead.
CAC scoring refines intermediate-risk decisions, not the management of a very high-risk patient already on therapy.

questions.q: A patient taking atorvastatin reports severe muscle pain, weakness, and dark tea-colored urine. What is the priority concern?
ch: Tendon rupture, the characteristic risk of bempedoic acid therapy
Statin hepatotoxicity, which baseline LFTs would have predicted
Dehydration producing concentrated but otherwise normal urine
Rhabdomyolysis — a red flag requiring immediate evaluation
Ordinary statin-associated muscle symptoms; continue unchanged
questions.exp: Severe muscle pain and weakness with dark tea-colored urine on a statin is the red flag for rhabdomyolysis. Statin-associated muscle symptoms are common and true rhabdomyolysis is rare, but CK should be checked whenever the patient is symptomatic.
why: Tendon rupture risk belongs to bempedoic acid, and this patient is taking a statin.
Baseline LFTs are checked with statins, but hepatotoxicity does not present as muscle pain with dark urine.
Dehydration does not explain severe muscle pain and weakness in a patient on a statin.
Common statin-associated muscle symptoms do not include weakness with dark urine; that combination demands evaluation.

questions.q: How is the coronary artery calcium (CAC) score best used in lipid management?
ch: To reclassify intermediate-risk patients when the statin treatment decision is uncertain
To replace the lipid panel as the primary screening test for dyslipidemia
To confirm familial hypercholesterolemia in a patient with tendon xanthomas
To monitor the response to therapy every three months after starting a statin
To decide whether triglyceride lowering is needed to prevent acute pancreatitis
questions.exp: CAC scoring reclassifies intermediate-risk patients and personalizes the statin decision when treatment decisions are uncertain; a score of zero can reasonably defer statins in selected intermediate-risk patients.
why: The lipid panel remains the core test; CAC refines risk rather than replacing screening.
Familial hypercholesterolemia is suspected from LDL-C of 190 or higher, family history, and exam findings.
CAC is not a monitoring tool; follow-up lipid panels 4 to 12 weeks after a change serve that purpose.
Pancreatitis risk is judged from the triglyceride level itself, not from a calcium score.

questions.q: A previously well patient is found to have new, marked hyperlipidemia. Which workup best screens for secondary causes?
ch: Abdominal ultrasound and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
A genetic panel for PCSK9 gain-of-function mutations in every patient
TSH, fasting glucose or HbA1c, renal and liver panel, and urine protein
Coronary angiography together with an exercise treadmill test
Serum CK and an electromyogram of the proximal muscle groups
questions.exp: Screening for secondary causes means TSH, fasting glucose or HbA1c, renal and liver panel, and urine protein — capturing hypothyroidism, diabetes, nephrotic syndrome, and cholestasis, alongside a review of drugs such as thiazides and steroids.
why: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring addresses hypertension, not secondary dyslipidemia.
Genetic testing of every patient is not the screening strategy; familial disease is suspected from LDL-C and family history.
Coronary testing evaluates established disease, not the secondary causes of the lipid abnormality.
CK and electromyography evaluate muscle symptoms on therapy, not secondary causes of hyperlipidemia.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the pathophysiology of GERD?
ch: Excess gastrin from a neuroendocrine tumor drives acid hypersecretion and ulceration
An incompetent or transiently relaxing lower esophageal sphincter allows reflux that overwhelms esophageal clearance and mucosal defense
Autoimmune destruction of the gastric parietal cells eliminates acid secretion entirely
Loss of myenteric ganglion cells prevents the lower esophageal sphincter from ever relaxing
Eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal mucosa produces rings, furrows, and dysphagia
questions.exp: GERD arises from an incompetent or transiently relaxing lower esophageal sphincter that lets acidic reflux, along with bile and pepsin, overwhelm esophageal clearance and mucosal defense — it is a barrier failure, not simply too much acid.
why: Gastrin-driven hypersecretion is a distinct rare entity; GERD is failure of the antireflux barrier.
Loss of parietal cells causes achlorhydria, essentially the opposite of acid reflux disease.
Failure of the sphincter to relax describes achalasia, which manometry is used to rule out.
Eosinophilic infiltration with rings and furrows is eosinophilic esophagitis, a mimic of GERD.

questions.q: Why is a proton pump inhibitor taken 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast?
ch: It forms a floating raft over the gastric contents before the meal arrives
Fasting administration avoids interference with calcium and magnesium absorption
PPIs bind only actively secreting proton pumps, and the meal stimulates secretion
Food destroys the drug, so it can only be given on a completely empty stomach
Morning dosing prevents the tachyphylaxis that develops with regular use
questions.exp: PPI timing matters because PPIs bind only actively secreting proton pumps, so the dose is given before the first meal; full benefit takes several days, and the drug should not be treated like an on-demand antacid.
why: Forming a floating raft is how alginate works, and alginate is best taken after meals.
Mineral malabsorption is a long-term PPI concern, not the reason for dosing before breakfast.
PPIs are not destroyed by food; the timing exists to catch actively secreting pumps.
Tachyphylaxis develops with H2 receptor antagonists such as famotidine, not from PPI timing.

questions.q: Endoscopy in a patient with long-standing reflux shows salmon-colored mucosa in the distal esophagus. What confirms Barrett's esophagus, and why does it matter?
ch: Intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells on biopsy; it is the key premalignant lesion
Eosinophils above 15 per high-power field; it predicts failure of acid suppression
Los Angeles grade D erosions; they establish irreversible sphincter incompetence
Absent peristalsis on manometry; it confirms progression toward achalasia
A positive H. pylori stain; it identifies the organism driving the reflux
questions.exp: Barrett's esophagus is salmon-colored mucosa with intestinal metaplasia and goblet cells on biopsy — the key premalignant lesion on the pathway from chronic reflux through dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma.
why: Dense esophageal eosinophilia defines eosinophilic esophagitis, a separate diagnosis.
The Los Angeles grades describe the severity of erosive esophagitis, not Barrett's metaplasia.
Absent peristalsis suggests achalasia, which manometry is used to exclude before surgery.
H. pylori is tested for when dyspepsia overlaps, but it does not define Barrett's esophagus.

questions.q: Which finding in a patient with reflux symptoms mandates prompt upper endoscopy instead of an empiric PPI trial?
ch: Regurgitation of sour fluid a few times each week after dinner
Dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, anemia, or new onset over age 60
Heartburn that is worse after large meals and when lying supine
A hiatal hernia noted incidentally on a previous chest radiograph
Symptoms that respond within three days of starting famotidine
questions.exp: Alarm features — dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleed, anemia, vomiting, and new onset over age 60 — mandate prompt EGD; uncomplicated classic symptoms are handled with an empiric PPI trial.
why: Occasional sour regurgitation without alarm features does not by itself require endoscopy.
Postprandial and supine heartburn is the classic uncomplicated picture treated with an empiric trial.
An incidental hiatal hernia predisposes to reflux but is not synonymous with GERD and is not an alarm feature.
A prompt response to acid suppression is reassuring and is not an indication for endoscopy.

questions.q: How is erosive esophagitis graded, and what does a normal endoscopy in a symptomatic patient suggest?
ch: Prague C and M criteria; a normal endoscopy points to functional dyspepsia only
Savary-Miller stages 1 to 5; a normal endoscopy indicates achalasia is present
Barrett's dysplasia grading; a normal endoscopy rules out pathologic acid exposure
Los Angeles grades A to D; a normal endoscopy suggests non-erosive reflux disease
Los Angeles grades I to IV; a normal endoscopy excludes reflux disease entirely
questions.exp: Erosive esophagitis is graded by the Los Angeles classification A to D, and non-erosive reflux disease often has a normal endoscopy despite genuine reflux symptoms.
why: The Prague criteria describe the extent of Barrett's, not the grade of erosive esophagitis.
Erosive disease is graded by the Los Angeles classification, and a normal study does not mean achalasia.
Dysplasia grading applies to Barrett's biopsies; a normal endoscopy is entirely compatible with NERD.
The Los Angeles system uses letters A to D, and a normal endoscopy does not exclude reflux.

questions.q: Which set of lifestyle measures is recommended for reflux?
ch: Increased caffeine and alcohol intake to stimulate lower esophageal sphincter tone
Sleeping completely flat without a pillow and eating the largest meal just before bed
Routine NSAID use with meals plus a calcium channel blocker to relax the sphincter
Weight loss, elevating the head of the bed 6 to 8 inches, and avoiding meals within 3 hours of lying down
Large evening meals followed by supine rest to help the stomach empty more completely
questions.exp: Lifestyle modification for reflux means weight loss, elevating the head of the bed 6 to 8 inches, avoiding meals within 3 hours of lying down, smaller meals, limiting trigger foods, and smoking and alcohol cessation.
why: Caffeine and alcohol are provocants of reflux; the advice is to limit them, not increase them.
Sleeping flat and eating just before bed are exactly the behaviors patients are taught to avoid.
NSAIDs and calcium channel blockers are cautioned against because they aggravate reflux or lower LES tone.
Large evening meals followed by lying down provoke reflux rather than relieving it.

questions.q: Before anti-reflux surgery, which tests objectively confirm the diagnosis and assess motility?
ch: Ambulatory pH monitoring with impedance, plus esophageal manometry
A barium swallow alone, repeated after an eight-week course of therapy
H. pylori stool antigen testing and a fasting serum gastrin level
Coronary angiography to exclude a cardiac cause of the chest pain
Capsule endoscopy of the small bowel with mucosal biopsy sampling
questions.exp: Ambulatory pH monitoring, with or without impedance, is the gold standard for confirming pathologic acid exposure before anti-reflux surgery, and esophageal manometry assesses motility and LES function while ruling out achalasia.
why: A barium swallow does not quantify acid exposure or assess esophageal motility.
H. pylori and gastrin testing address other diagnoses, not preoperative reflux confirmation.
Cardiac testing is considered when atypical chest pain overlaps, not as preoperative reflux assessment.
Capsule endoscopy examines the small bowel and has no role in preoperative reflux evaluation.

questions.q: A patient with 15 years of heartburn now reports new solid-food dysphagia. What must be considered until proven otherwise?
ch: Functional heartburn, best managed with reassurance and further observation
A hiatal hernia, which is synonymous with GERD and needs no further workup
Peptic stricture or Barrett's with adenocarcinoma, requiring urgent endoscopy
Tachyphylaxis to famotidine, managed by switching him to an antacid
Hypomagnesemia from chronic acid suppression, corrected by supplementation
questions.exp: New dysphagia on a background of long-standing GERD means peptic stricture or Barrett's and adenocarcinoma until proven otherwise; dysphagia is an alarm feature that requires urgent EGD.
why: Functional heartburn is a diagnosis of exclusion and never explains a new alarm feature.
A hiatal hernia predisposes to reflux but is not synonymous with GERD and does not account for dysphagia.
Tachyphylaxis to an H2 blocker does not cause dysphagia, and switching to an antacid ignores an alarm feature.
Hypomagnesemia is a long-term PPI effect and does not produce solid-food dysphagia.

questions.q: A 24-year-old has reflux symptoms that do not respond to a full-dose PPI. What should be considered next?
ch: Doubling the PPI dose indefinitely without any further evaluation
Immediate fundoplication regardless of objective reflux testing
Long-term metoclopramide as first-line maintenance monotherapy
Antacids alone, on the reasoning that acid is clearly not involved
Eosinophilic esophagitis — endoscopy with biopsy is warranted
questions.exp: Refractory reflux unresponsive to PPIs in a young patient should raise eosinophilic esophagitis, and biopsy is warranted; functional heartburn is the other mimic, and simply up-dosing acid suppression misses both.
why: Escalating the dose indefinitely without evaluation is exactly the reflex to avoid in a PPI non-responder.
Surgery requires objective reflux documented by pH or impedance testing and adequate motility first.
Metoclopramide is a short-course adjunct for delayed gastric emptying, limited by tardive dyskinesia.
Antacids give only brief on-demand relief and do not address the cause of PPI non-response.

questions.q: Which risks justify using the lowest effective PPI dose and reassessing therapy periodically?
ch: Tardive dyskinesia and extrapyramidal symptoms with prolonged therapy
Dental erosions and hoarseness, which are extraesophageal reflux effects
Constipation with aluminum salts and diarrhea with magnesium salts
Hypergastrinemia that reliably progresses to esophageal adenocarcinoma
Hypomagnesemia, B12 and iron malabsorption, C. difficile, and fractures
questions.exp: Long-term PPI risks include hypomagnesemia, B12 and iron malabsorption, C. difficile, and fractures — so the lowest effective dose is used and therapy is reassessed, with monitoring of magnesium and B12.
why: Tardive dyskinesia and extrapyramidal symptoms are metoclopramide risks, not PPI risks.
Dental erosions and hoarseness are extraesophageal manifestations of reflux itself, not effects of PPI therapy.
Constipation with aluminum and diarrhea with magnesium are antacid effects, not PPI effects.
Hypergastrinemia is monitored with vonoprazan, and it does not reliably progress to adenocarcinoma.
